frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a major market for Algerian gas, creating leverage but also exposure to price volatility and shifting demand. Algeria is balancing export commitments with domestic energy subsidies and consumption.

frictionVectors.title: Sahara security and border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Libya, Mali, and the Sahel increases surveillance and defense costs along Algeria's southern borders. External security partnerships remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and oil-service firms retain substantial influence over production, technology, and export logistics. Declining output and price swings constrain Luanda's room for sovereign investment.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked financing and major infrastructure relationships remain important, even as Angola seeks broader partners and improved debt management. Strategic transport and energy projects can create long-term repayment exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port and trade corridors remain vulnerable to regional competition, customs disruption, and dependence on external logistics capital. Connectivity with Nigeria and the Sahel is economically valuable but politically exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders is forcing greater reliance on international security assistance and domestic security spending. Persistent insecurity threatens transport, agriculture, and extractive investment.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong negotiating leverage over diamond extraction and marketing, but remains exposed to synthetic stones, weak global demand, and the commercial fortunes of major partners.

frictionVectors.title: Diversification and water constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water availability, a small domestic market, and dependence on regional trade complicate efforts to convert mineral wealth into broader industrial capacity. External capital is useful but must be aligned with national development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control over gold and mining revenues while relying on external security relationships, including ties with Russian-linked actors. This can reduce Western influence but risks opaque contracts and dependency on a new partner.

frictionVectors.title: Mining disruption from insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks and insecurity threaten mine sites, transport corridors, and artisanal mining communities. Resource nationalism cannot fully translate into sovereign control without improved territorial security and administrative reach.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater value from nickel and other mineral projects, but financing, processing capacity, and foreign-investor dependence limit effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Transit Friction
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain tense, complicating cross-border commerce and regional infrastructure access while increasing Burundi's dependence on alternative corridors through Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Port and Logistics Assets
frictionVectors.details: Port expansion and logistics development rely heavily on external capital and operators, creating long-term leverage risks despite improved infrastructure and connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Maritime Surveillance
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde depends on European and wider international partners for maritime domain awareness, fisheries enforcement, and counter-narcotics capacity across its extensive waters.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Concession Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to Cameroon’s hydrocarbons, mining, and infrastructure sectors, while limited domestic processing reduces the state’s ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Chad-Cameroon Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts state authority and investment, while insecurity around transport routes and the northern border raises costs for major pipeline and trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Linkage
frictionVectors.details: The government’s security relationship with Russian personnel is closely associated with protection of political power and access to gold and other minerals, limiting transparency and bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Dependence and Armed-Group Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states exposes the country to border insecurity, high transport costs, and external control over the movement of commercial goods.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the central source of export earnings and fiscal power, but dependence on foreign operators, volatile prices, and opaque revenue management weakens broad-based sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Sudan Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability around Libya, Sudan, and the Lake Chad Basin forces heavy security spending and sustains reliance on external military and diplomatic partners, even as foreign basing arrangements evolve.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and French Influence
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute sustains diplomatic friction with France, while French economic and security ties remain important to Comoros. The issue is also politically useful for domestic mobilization.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros seeks to expand maritime infrastructure but remains dependent on external lenders, contractors, and imported fuel. Limited fiscal capacity constrains sovereign control over strategic connectivity projects.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-linked investors retain substantial influence over cobalt and copper production, refining, and logistics. Kinshasa is pressing for greater value addition and contract leverage but faces financing and technical constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Conflict and Regional Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine territorial sovereignty and disrupt mineral corridors. Relations with Rwanda and Uganda remain highly sensitive, while international mediation has produced limited security gains.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and export capacity remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price swings and external operators. Limited diversification weakens bargaining power over long-term resource terms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction partnerships remain important for roads, ports, and energy infrastructure. Debt obligations and project concentration can narrow the government's room to set independent economic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value-Chain Control
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is seeking greater domestic processing and stronger farmer incomes, but foreign traders and manufacturers still capture much of the value. Exposure to global prices and climate stress limits policy gains.

frictionVectors.title: French and Western Security Ties
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is diversifying partnerships while retaining significant French, European, and Western commercial and security links. Regional instability in the Sahel creates pressure to protect northern borders and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Base Concentration and Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities from the United States, China, France, Japan, and others, providing revenue and security but limiting strategic autonomy. Competition among external powers increases the country's geopolitical exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and transport links remain closely tied to external operators, creditors, and Ethiopia's trade flows. Debt pressures and the loss of some commercial concessions have highlighted the limits of Djibouti's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over state assets, currency policy, and major infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian dam operations, while diplomatic talks have not produced a binding water-sharing framework.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and weak new investment are eroding export capacity, increasing dependence on foreign operators and opaque production-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Offshore assets remain exposed to piracy and regional instability, requiring continued cooperation with foreign security and energy partners.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's proximity to Yemen and major shipping lanes draws competing regional interest while increasing pressure over port access and security alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production provides revenue, but foreign technical and capital requirements limit complete national control over extraction and exports.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and revenue concentration
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's fiscal stability remains tied to South African supply chains and Southern African Customs Union transfers, limiting independent economic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and water vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on regional electricity imports and shared water systems exposes national infrastructure to South African grid and drought conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access competition
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable port access drives negotiations and rivalries involving Somaliland, Somalia, Djibouti, Gulf states, and Turkey.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external financing constrain sovereign control over transport, energy, and telecommunications infrastructure despite stronger domestic leverage from GERD.

highlights: Oil and Manganese Remain Strategic Anchors

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International operators retain major influence over manganese, iron ore, and oil logistics. Libreville is seeking greater state participation and local processing without disrupting investment flows.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors remain essential to resource revenue and are vulnerable to dependence on foreign capital, contractors, and shipping networks.

highlights: Fisheries and Tourism Drive External Exposure

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Security and Economic Influence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional security, trade access, and transport connectivity. This dependence limits Banjul's room for maneuver on border, fisheries, and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries Governance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak enforcement threaten domestic food security and coastal livelihoods. Licensing transparency remains a recurring sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and Gold-Sector Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining, environmental damage, and illicit gold flows continue to challenge state control despite stronger enforcement. Foreign-backed equipment and informal networks complicate accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is pressing for domestic processing and tighter control over lithium and other strategic minerals. Competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf interests are increasing pressure on licensing and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou project could transform Guinea's fiscal and logistical position, but rail, port, and financing arrangements remain heavily dependent on multinational consortia and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and Mining Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using mining permits and infrastructure demands to increase state control while delaying a full political transition. Contract uncertainty raises friction with investors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Raw cashew exports dominate rural incomes, while processing capacity and price-setting remain concentrated outside the country. This limits domestic value capture and fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Trafficking, and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested political authority leave maritime infrastructure vulnerable to external commercial pressure and illicit trafficking networks. Security partnerships can provide stability but also constrain sovereign control.

highlights: Debt diplomacy tightens room for maneuver

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large Chinese-financed infrastructure obligations constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Debt-service pressures are increasing scrutiny of foreign-built transport and energy projects.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa's role as an East African gateway faces competition from regional corridors and outside-backed port projects. Control of customs, rail, and logistics contracts remains a sovereignty-sensitive issue.

highlights: Water exports anchor dependence on South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Water sovereignty and revenue exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's strategic water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on its larger neighbor. Pricing, royalties, and dam ownership remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Phase II infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project brings major infrastructure and construction benefits while exposing the country to external financiers, contractors, and project delays. Local participation and benefit-sharing remain contested.

highlights: Resource governance enters a reform window
Concessions still dominate the economic landscape

frictionVectors.title: Mining and concession renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, rubber, and potential offshore resources remain controlled largely through foreign-led concessions. Monrovia faces pressure to increase local value addition, tax collection, and transparency without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financiers remain central to port, road, and mining-corridor development. Limited state capacity makes infrastructure contracts a continuing channel for outside influence.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival authorities
Foreign patrons shape security and energy access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Competing eastern and western power centers continue to contest appointments, budgets, and access around the National Oil Corporation. Export disruptions remain a persistent tool of political bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: External military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf actors, and European states retain influence through security partnerships, mercenary networks, migration policy, and energy interests. Their involvement limits the prospects for unified sovereign control.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external interests
Energy and transport gaps weaken bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence and value leakage
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and illicitly traded precious stones draw foreign capital while domestic processing remains limited. Tax disputes, environmental costs, and weak oversight reduce Madagascar's leverage over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and power vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and inadequate transport networks increase dependence on foreign lenders, contractors, and mining-linked infrastructure. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, European, and other investors is reshaping strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and bilateral creditors limit Malawi's room to set independent fiscal and resource policies.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: New mining projects, including uranium and rare-earth prospects, attract foreign capital faster than domestic regulatory and value-addition capacity is developing.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support increases Moscow's leverage while offering limited resolution to Mali's insurgency and governance crisis.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking greater control and revenue from gold operations, raising tensions with international mining companies and investors.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens Mauritania's finances but leaves key export infrastructure and technical capacity tied to foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Corridor Governance
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore railways, ports, fisheries, and prospective green-hydrogen projects are attracting outside capital faster than domestic processing and local-benefit mechanisms.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty Transition
frictionVectors.details: The future governance and security arrangements around the Chagos Archipelago remain strategically sensitive because of the Diego Garcia military facility.

frictionVectors.title: Port Influence Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance Indian, Chinese, European, and regional interest in its ports and maritime infrastructure without compromising strategic neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara remain contested, exposing phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure projects to legal and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding ports, energy links, and industrial corridors while managing competing European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. interests.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG restart remains pivotal
Gas revenues face sovereignty and security tests

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy firms and international security support remain central to restarting Cabo Delgado projects. This limits Maputo's immediate control over gas infrastructure and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks continue to threaten transport corridors, communities, and offshore-linked logistics. Persistent insecurity could delay investment and deepen reliance on external military assistance.

highlights: Green hydrogen ambitions attract major capital

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies are positioned to influence the development timetable and fiscal structure of new offshore discoveries. Namibia is seeking stronger local benefits while avoiding investor flight.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed hydrogen projects could accelerate industrialization but may leave Namibia dependent on external finance, technology, and export infrastructure.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Re renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is revising arrangements with foreign mining interests and seeking greater state control. Reduced Western engagement and sanctions complicate technology, finance, and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil export corridor and regional trade routes remain vulnerable to political isolation, insecurity, and disputes with neighboring states. Dependence on alternative external partners is increasing.

highlights: Oil-sector reform seeks stronger state capture
Dangote and gas investment deepen industrial capacity

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Control Contest
frictionVectors.details: The government is trying to raise production and reduce dependence on international oil majors while managing opaque licensing, subsidy, and fiscal pressures. Production losses and theft still weaken sovereign resource capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, weak transmission, and financing constraints limit the conversion of gas reserves into reliable domestic power. Foreign capital remains important for major LNG and infrastructure projects.

highlights: Regional security posture drives external scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Traceability
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional tantalum and tin supply chains attracts scrutiny over the origin and transit of minerals linked to eastern DRC. Compliance pressure from Western buyers and neighboring governments could constrain Kigali's commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Security
frictionVectors.details: Accusations of support for M23 have intensified diplomatic and economic pressure, including demands for withdrawal and sanctions risk. The confrontation threatens regional trade access and Rwanda's investor-friendly reputation.

highlights: Offshore oil remains prospective, not yet transformative

frictionVectors.title: Unproven Offshore Hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: International operators retain interest in São Tomé and Príncipe's offshore blocks, but the absence of commercial production limits state leverage. Contract transparency and revenue expectations remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign assistance and outside investment for ports, energy, and maritime security. China, Portugal, and other partners compete for influence without any single actor fully dominating.

highlights: First-wave oil and gas production reshapes state leverage

frictionVectors.title: Sangomar and GTA Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas revenues give Dakar greater bargaining power over operators, but efforts to increase the state's share risk investor disputes and delays. Governance of the Senegal-Mauritania GTA project remains particularly politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Funded Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, railways, energy, and urban infrastructure depend on external finance from Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral partners. Rising debt constrains the government's ability to convert resource wealth into fully autonomous development policy.

highlights: Foreign fleets still dominate tuna value chains

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fisheries Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles controls a strategically important maritime zone but captures limited value from industrial tuna fishing conducted by foreign fleets. Licensing, monitoring, and port infrastructure remain central tests of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, France, and other partners seek maritime access and security cooperation around the archipelago. Victoria generally balances these relationships, but infrastructure and surveillance projects can create political sensitivities.

highlights: Mining revival increases foreign capital exposure
Infrastructure corridors outrun local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Rutile Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, while foreign operators retain significant control over capital, logistics, and marketing. Contract terms, environmental impacts, and local employment continue to generate sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors are involved in mining, transport, energy, and port-related projects. These links can improve infrastructure but risk reinforcing a model in which raw materials leave the country with limited domestic processing.

highlights: Offshore hydrocarbons become a federal flashpoint
Security and port access remain externally managed

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Licensing Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Federal efforts to attract offshore exploration are constrained by disputes with member states over licensing authority and revenue sharing. Weak institutional capacity and insecurity increase the risk that future resource deals will be negotiated asymmetrically.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners shape Somalia's security assistance, port access, and maritime infrastructure. Rival external relationships intersect with federal-regional tensions, limiting unified national control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: MINING OWNERSHIP AND BENEFICIATION
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and local value capture from platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals. Investment, regulatory uncertainty and continued foreign corporate participation constrain the pace of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: ELECTRICITY AND PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Power-generation weakness and deteriorating rail and port capacity undermine mineral exports and industrial sovereignty. Private investment and foreign technical support are increasingly necessary to stabilize core infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE AND OIL REVENUE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on oil exports through Sudan, leaving production and public finances vulnerable to conflict, pipeline damage and bargaining pressure from transit authorities. Chinese and other foreign operators remain central to the upstream and transport system.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Political and military elites continue to depend on neighboring states and external partners for mediation, logistics and security support. This limits independent management of oil revenues and border resources.

highlights: Gold economy fuels competing power centers

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING AND EXTERNAL SPONSORSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade are being used to finance rival wartime networks, with regional and international intermediaries competing for access. Weak state oversight allows external actors to capture substantial value.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND OIL CORRIDOR VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, refineries and transit routes is strategically contested as the conflict disrupts national logistics. Damage or political blockage along the South Sudan oil corridor would further erode central fiscal capacity.

highlights: Ports and minerals draw strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS AND LOCAL VALUE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing mining companies for higher state participation, domestic processing and improved fiscal returns, especially in gold and critical minerals. Negotiations with foreign investors remain a recurring source of legal and political friction.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam port and regional transport corridors are attracting Gulf, Chinese and other foreign capital. These investments improve connectivity but raise concerns over long-term control of strategic infrastructure and neighboring-market access.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port is central to national revenue and Sahel trade, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign operators, financiers and shipping networks. External commercial influence can narrow policy autonomy despite strong state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a strategic national asset, yet production constraints, financing needs and limited downstream processing reduce domestic value capture. The government must balance sovereignty goals against reliance on external technology and capital.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and migration support gives Brussels significant leverage over Tunisia's border policy and domestic security choices. Tunis seeks funding without accepting extensive external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons and constrained power infrastructure limits Tunisia's economic autonomy. Delays in renewable and grid investment increase exposure to European suppliers and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces Western political, legal, and financing opposition. Chinese and Gulf-linked capital have become increasingly important alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Transit Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's future petroleum revenues depend on Tanzanian transit infrastructure and regional stability. This creates external leverage over export timing, costs, and project security.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to seek greater domestic processing and fiscal returns from copper and cobalt. Bargaining power remains constrained by capital needs and established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and drought-related generation losses threaten mines, manufacturing, and export reliability. Emergency imports and new private generation increase infrastructure dependence while reforms remain incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Processing Control
frictionVectors.details: Harare is tightening restrictions on raw lithium and other mineral exports to capture more value domestically. Limited power, finance, and refining capacity leave the country reliant on foreign firms to develop processing.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Investment Channels
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance push Zimbabwe toward Chinese, Gulf, and other non-Western investors. This expands policy room but can reinforce opaque contracts and asymmetric resource deals.
